statement: The first-loss piece of a securitization is also called the equity piece.
explanation: The most junior note absorbs losses first and is usually held by the originator, so it is also called the equity piece (equity tranche), even though it is a bond.
originalText: Equity piece

statement: The equity class created by overcollateralization is typically rated AAA because it is backed by the largest share of collateral.
explanation: The equity (first-loss) class is the most junior class and is typically non-rated or lowest-rated; AAA describes the senior class.
originalText: It is rated AAA because it is backed by the largest share of collateral
correction: The equity class created by overcollateralization is typically non-rated, as it is the most junior class and absorbs losses first.

changes.from: rated AAA because it is backed by the largest share of collateral
changes.to: non-rated, as it is the most junior class and absorbs losses first

statement: The equity class created by overcollateralization is typically retained by the originator.
explanation: The originator typically keeps the first-loss (equity) piece of a securitization.
originalText: It is typically retained by the originator

statement: The equity class created by overcollateralization is typically non-rated.
explanation: The first-loss piece is the lowest credit quality class and is often not rated.
originalText: It is typically non‑rated

statement: The equity class of a securitization absorbs the first losses on the asset pool.
explanation: First-loss means the class is hit by losses before any other class.
originalText: It absorbs the first losses on the asset pool

statement: Overcollateralization is equal to zero when the nominal value of the credit-sensitive assets in the collateral pool equals the nominal value of the issued securities.
explanation: Overcollateralization is the nominal value of the pool assets minus the nominal value of the issued securities, so equality gives zero.
originalText: Over‑collateralization

statement: Excess spread is equal to zero whenever the nominal value of the collateral pool equals the nominal value of the issued securities.
explanation: Excess spread depends on the asset yield compared with the interest cost of the notes, not on whether nominal values are equal; it is overcollateralization that is zero in that case.
originalText: Excess spread

statement: The risk that the originator typically retains in a securitization is the first-loss piece.
explanation: Originators usually keep the most junior, lowest-quality class, which absorbs the initial losses of the pool.
originalText: First‑loss piece

statement: Securitizing long- and medium-term loans increases the average duration of a bank's balance sheet assets.
explanation: The loans leave the balance sheet and are replaced by cash, so securitization shortens average asset duration and reduces funding and duration mismatch.
originalText: Increase average duration of balance sheet assets
correction: Securitizing long- and medium-term loans reduces the average duration of a bank's balance sheet assets.

statement: Securitization allows a bank to diversify its funding mix.
explanation: Selling loans to an SPV that issues notes adds a new source of funding.
originalText: Diversify its funding mix

statement: Securitization can increase a bank's return on equity by removing assets from the balance sheet and so reducing required capital.
explanation: Removing assets lowers the regulatory capital needed, so the equity base shrinks relative to earnings and ROE rises.
originalText: Increase return on equity (ROE)

statement: Securitization allows a bank to remove certain credit risks from its balance sheet.
explanation: Credit risk on the transferred loans moves to the SPV and the note investors, apart from any piece the originator retains.
originalText: Remove certain credit risks from the balance sheet

statement: The funding cost of a securitization can still be lower than the originator's own bond funding, because the notes are rated on the quality of the asset pool and are typically rated higher than the originator's bonds.
explanation: Securitization de-links the notes' rating from the originator's rating. The higher rating frequently outweighs the illiquidity premium of the ABS market.
originalText: The cost can still be lower because the notes are rated on the quality of the asset pool, and are typically rated higher than the bank’s own bonds.

statement: The lower liquidity of ABS always outweighs any rating advantage over the originator's own bonds, so securitization funding is always more costly.
explanation: Lower liquidity adds to the ABS yield, but the higher rating of the notes frequently outweighs it, so the originator's funding cost is often lower through securitization.
originalText: The cost will be higher because illiquidity always outweighs any difference in credit ratings between the ABS and the originator’s bonds.

statement: The notes issued by an SPV carry no credit risk once the loans are transferred, which is why securitization funding costs less.
explanation: The notes still carry the credit risk of the asset pool, absorbed through tranching and credit enhancement; the lower cost comes from their higher rating.
originalText: The cost will be lower because the SPV is not subject to any credit risk once the loans are transferred.

statement: The notes issued by an SPV carry the originator's credit rating, so securitization funding costs the same as the originator's own bond funding.
explanation: The notes' rating is de-linked from the originator's rating and depends on the asset pool and structure; this is the main source of the funding benefit.
originalText: The cost will be the same because the ABS carry the originator’s credit rating, which is applied to all notes issued by the SPV.

statement: When a bank securitizes a loan pool and retains the first-loss piece, regulatory capital requirements on the pool are significantly reduced but not eliminated, and ROE is likely to improve.
explanation: The retained first-loss piece keeps a capital charge with the bank, so relief is large but partial. Lower capital needs reduce equity issuance and raise ROE.
originalText: Regulatory capital requirements on the pool are significantly reduced but not eliminated, and ROE is likely to improve.

statement: Regulatory capital requirements on a securitized loan pool fall to zero because the SPV is not a bank, even if the originator retains the first-loss piece.
explanation: A retained first-loss piece keeps part of the exposure and its capital charge with the originator, so capital relief is large but not complete.
originalText: Regulatory capital requirements on the pool fall to zero because the SPV is not a bank, and ROE rises.

statement: Securitization reduces regulatory capital requirements but lowers ROE, because the originator must issue more preferred stock to replace the capital released.
explanation: Securitization reduces the need to issue preferred stock and other equity, so ROE increases rather than declines.
originalText: Regulatory capital requirements fall, but ROE declines because the bank must now issue more preferred stock to replace the capital released.

statement: Pool insurance is a credit enhancement provided by a third-party insurer outside the SPV.
explanation: Pool insurance is a policy from an outside insurer covering loss of principal in the collateral pool, whereas overcollateralization, excess spread and subordination are built into the pool and note structure.
originalText: Pool insurance

statement: Overcollateralization arises when the nominal value of the assets in the pool is greater than the nominal value of the issued securities.
explanation: The excess collateral gives a first cushion that absorbs initial losses before investors are affected.
originalText: Over‑collateralization

statement: Excess spread is the difference between the return on the underlying assets and the interest rate payable on the issued notes.
explanation: Excess spread is asset return less note interest. It is available to absorb expenses and losses, and any surplus is held in a reserve account.
originalText: Excess spread

statement: Overcollateralization is the difference between the return on the underlying assets and the interest rate payable on the issued notes.
explanation: Overcollateralization is a balance-based cushion, where the assets exceed the notes in nominal value; the return difference is excess spread.
originalText: Over‑collateralization

statement: A margin step-up, in which the coupon increases after a call date, is sometimes used by asset-backed securities.
explanation: A margin step-up raises the coupon after the call date, an incentive for the issuer to call and for investors to hold.
originalText: A margin step‑up is sometimes used by asset‑backed securities (ABSs) where the coupon structure increases after a call date.

statement: Credit enhancements are typically associated only with mortgage-backed securities and are not used in other types of asset-backed securities.
explanation: Credit enhancements are used across both ABS and MBS structures.
originalText: Credit enhancements are typically only associated with mortgage‑backed securities (MBSs) and are not used in other types of asset‑backed securities (ABSs).

statement: The most senior class of notes is often overcollateralized in order to reduce the risk of the asset-backed security.
explanation: Overcollateralization protects the lowest (junior) class of notes, which absorbs losses first, not the senior class.
originalText: The most senior class of notes is often overcollateralized in order to reduce the risk of the asset‑backed security (ABS).

statement: In a securitization structured through an SPV, the asset side of the SPV has a lower cost than the liability side.
explanation: The structure is built so that the liabilities (notes) cost less than the asset yield, which produces excess spread.
originalText: The securitization process is structured such that the asset side of the SPV has a lower cost than the liability side of the SPV.

statement: An early amortization trigger in a revolving securitization ends the revolving period early and begins returning principal to investors, protecting them from further deterioration in the pool.
explanation: When a threshold such as the monthly payment rate is breached, reinvestment stops and principal collections are passed to noteholders, shortening the notes' life.
originalText: The trigger ends the revolving period early and begins returning principal to investors, protecting them from further deterioration in the pool.

statement: An early amortization trigger tied to a fall in the monthly payment rate allows the originator to extend the revolving period so that the pool can recover.
explanation: The trigger shortens the revolving period rather than extending it: reinvestment stops and principal is returned to investors.
originalText: The trigger allows the originator to extend the revolving period if the MPR deteriorates, giving the pool time to recover.

statement: An early amortization trigger converts a revolving securitization to an amortizing one while leaving the expected weighted-average life of the notes unchanged.
explanation: Amortizing early repays principal sooner, so the expected weighted-average life of the notes shortens.
originalText: The trigger converts the transaction from a revolving to an amortizing structure while leaving the expected weighted‑average life of the notes unchanged.

statement: Because CMBS loans are non-recourse and fully secured by the underlying property, the debt service coverage ratio (DSCR) is crucial for evaluating their credit risk.
explanation: With non-recourse loans the lender can look only to the property, so repayment depends on the cash the property generates, which DSCR (net operating income / debt payments) captures.
originalText: CMBS loans are non‑recourse because they are fully secured by the underlying property, so the debt service coverage ratio (DSCR) becomes crucial for evaluating credit risk.

statement: CMBS loans are recourse to the borrower, so the delinquency ratio is the key performance measure for CMBS.
explanation: CMBS loans are non-recourse, secured only by the property, so DSCR is the key measure; the delinquency ratio is a credit card ABS measure.
originalText: CMBS loans are recourse to the borrower, so the delinquency ratio is the key performance measure.

statement: CMBS loans are non-recourse because they are only partly secured by the property, so the monthly payment rate (MPR) is crucial for evaluating their credit risk.
explanation: CMBS loans are fully secured by the property, and MPR is a credit card measure; DSCR is the crucial measure for CMBS.
originalText: CMBS loans are non‑recourse because they are only partly secured by the property, so the monthly payment rate (MPR) becomes crucial for evaluating credit risk.

statement: Single monthly mortality (SMM), the constant prepayment rate (CPR) and the Public Securities Association (PSA) rate are the measures most likely used for securitized products backed by student loans.
explanation: Student-loan pools prepay like mortgage pools, so SMM, CPR and the PSA benchmark are the standard prepayment tools.
originalText: Single monthly mortality (SMM), constant prepayment rate (CPR), and Public Securities Association (PSA) rate

statement: Loss curves and absolute prepayment speed (APS) are the measures most likely used for securitized products backed by student loans.
explanation: Loss curves and APS are used for auto-loan ABS; student loans are analysed with SMM, CPR and PSA.
originalText: Loss curves and absolute prepayment speed (APS)

statement: The debt service coverage ratio (DSCR) and the monthly payment rate (MPR) are the measures most likely used for securitized products backed by student loans.
explanation: DSCR is a commercial real estate measure and MPR a credit card measure; student loans use SMM, CPR and PSA.
originalText: Debt service coverage ratio (DSCR) and monthly payment rate (MPR)
